title: Danger recognition before the Assistant's turn
takeaway: Across ten prompts in which a user innocently narrates a hazardous situation, the words danger, unsafe, warning and toxic reach the top of the J-lens readout during the model's own response in both the base model and the post-trained model. Only the post-trained model ranks them at or near the top while it is still reading the user's message. The paper reads this as the same effect Figure 43 found for empathy, now for a second family of reactions.
walkthrough:
The figure extends the [[assistant-point-of-view]] result of section 6.1 to a second kind of reaction. Figure 43 tracked empathy; this one tracks the recognition of danger, on a different suite of prompts, with the same measurement and the same chart.

Ten prompts make up the danger awareness set. In each, the user narrates a hazardous situation without treating it as one — the paper's example is sanding old paint without a respirator. The hazard is never named in the prompt.

Four words are fixed in advance as the reaction concepts, following the [[reaction-concepts-protocol]]: danger, unsafe, warning and toxic. At every token the [[jacobian-lens]] ranks the whole vocabulary, and the best rank any of the four achieves is taken. That rank is then medianed over the [[workspace-layers]], roughly L38 to L92 on the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]] scale.

Each prompt is summarized by two numbers per model: the best rank reached anywhere in the user's turn, and the best rank reached anywhere in the model's own response.

### How to read the chart

Four bars stand in two pairs. The left pair is the user turn, the right pair the Assistant turn; within each pair the [[base-model]] sits beside the model built from it by [[post-training]]. The paper names the second only as a production post-trained model; the companion figure labels that series with a model name from the [[claude-model-family]].

The y axis is an inverted log scale of rank, so rank 1 is at the top and a taller bar means a better rank. Each bar's height is the geometric mean of the ten per-prompt ranks. One open circle per prompt is drawn on the bar, and hovering a circle opens that prompt with both models' [[j-lens-readout]] top-10 at its best position.

### What it shows

On the Assistant turn the two models sit close together, the four words near the top of the readout in both. The paper calls this expected, since both models' responses address the hazard.

On the user turn they separate. The post-trained model's [[j-space]] carries the safety assessment the [[assistant-persona]] would make, before the Assistant's turn has begun.

The paper hedges the base-model side: the concepts are "typically" not near the top there, not never. Ten prompts is a small suite, and the measurement is descriptive; nothing here tests whether the early content changes what either model writes.

terms.definition: The position of a token in the Jacobian lens's ranked list over the whole vocabulary, at one position and layer. Rank 1 means the lens scores that token above every other token there.

A short list of words fixed before any measurement, naming the reaction an Assistant would plausibly have to the prompt but which the prompt itself does not contain. The figure tracks only these words' ranks.
The four reaction concepts chosen for this suite. At each token the best rank achieved by any one of the four is the value carried forward.
The set of ten prompts behind this figure: a user narrates a hazardous situation innocently, such as sanding old paint without a respirator, without naming the hazard.
The pretrained model, trained only on next-token prediction, with no post-training. It is one series in each pair, and the lens is applied to it identically.

The production assistant model built from that base model by post-training. It is the other series in each pair; section 6.1 identifies it only as a production post-trained model, and the companion figure prints a product model name for it.
The left pair of bars. Its value is the best reaction-concept rank reached at any token of the user's message, before the model has begun to answer.
The right pair of bars. Its value is the best reaction-concept rank reached at any token of the model's own response.
The quantity the bars measure. The axis is inverted, so better — numerically smaller — ranks sit higher on the chart.

The rank axis is logarithmic and runs from the floor at the bottom to rank 1 at the top. Bars grow upward as ranks improve, and the gap between rank 1 and rank 5 gets as much room as the gap between 20 and 100.
Each bar's height. Ranks are multiplicative rather than additive quantities, so the ten per-prompt ranks are combined by geometric mean rather than an arithmetic average.
One small open circle per prompt, drawn on each bar at that prompt's own best rank, so the spread behind the geometric mean stays visible.
A faint line joining one prompt's base-model circle to its post-trained circle within the same turn, showing the per-prompt change rather than only the group means.
The bottom of the axis. A rank at or beyond it is clamped there and reported with a "≥" sign, since the exact value no longer carries information once a concept is far down the vocabulary.

The aggregation applied before ranks are compared across tokens: the reaction concepts' rank is taken at each layer in the workspace band, and the median across those layers is used, so a spike at one isolated layer does not count.
The middle band of depth in which the paper finds the J-space acting as a workspace, roughly L38 to L92. The lens is nearly empty before it, and collapses onto the imminent output after it.
The ten highest-ranked vocabulary tokens at the hovered prompt's best position, printed for both models, with any of the four reaction concepts highlighted.

The set of activations expressible as a sparse nonnegative combination of J-lens vectors — the region the paper argues acts as the model's workspace, and the thing the danger concepts are said to enter early.
The character the post-trained model speaks as. The claim here is that its safety assessment is present in the workspace before its turn starts.
Layer numbers on the paper's convention, where 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers are reindexed to 0–100 so a number reads as a percentage of depth.
The legend or caption note giving the number of prompts summarized. Each contributes one circle to each of the four bars.

numbers.meaning: The number of prompts in the danger awareness suite. Each contributes one circle per bar, and every bar is a geometric mean over these ten. The paper presents it as one of three small suites, not as a benchmark.
The number of reaction concepts fixed for this suite — danger, unsafe, warning, toxic. Fixing them in advance is what makes the rank comparable across prompts and across the two models.
The models compared under an identical lens: the pretrained base model and its post-trained counterpart. The contrast between them is the figure's whole point.
Two spans are summarized — the user turn and the Assistant turn — and each is split by model, giving four bars.

The layer band over which each token's reaction-concept rank is medianed, on the paper's 0–100 percent-of-depth scale. Section 4.1 identifies this range as the workspace layers: past the early layers where the J-space is empty, and before the final layers where readouts collapse onto the imminent output.

The best possible rank, at the top of the y axis. A prompt plotted at rank 1 means one of the four danger words was the single highest-scoring token in the lens readout at its best position in that turn.
The y-axis tick values. They are spaced logarithmically, so the visible distance between rank 1 and rank 2 is comparable to that between 50 and 100; the axis floor lies at or below the last tick.
The length of the ranked token list shown in the hover panel for each model. It is a display cutoff, not the measurement — the plotted rank is not capped at 10.
Context, not plotted here: the size of the bereavement suite in Figure 43, the figure this one repeats on a different reaction family.
Context, not plotted here: the size of the withheld answer suite in the companion Figure 81, the third of the three suites.

Context, not plotted here: the two Tylenol doses in the single-prompt example of section 6.1 that motivated this suite. On the 8000 mg overdose the post-trained model's readout at a token inside the user's sentence was unsafe, dangerous and WARNING; the base model's was pain, now and feels on both doses.
